Chapter 1, Fourier Series (printed pp. 1–64; PDF pp. 7–70): periodic signals, harmonic expansions, Hilbert-space structure, applications, and convergence.
1.1 Introduction and Choices to Make (printed p. 1; PDF p. 7): Fourier series as the periodic starting point; passage toward nonperiodic transforms; the spectrum principle.
1.2 Periodic Phenomena (printed pp. 2–3; PDF pp. 8–9): temporal and spatial periodicity, wave frequency and wavelength, crystal lattices, and oriented spatial frequencies.

1.3 Periodicity: Definitions, Examples, and Things to Come (printed pp. 4–8; PDF pp. 10–14): fundamental periods, sums and products of periodic functions, complex exponentials, eigenfunctions, orthogonality, and periodization.
1.4 It All Adds Up (printed p. 9; PDF p. 15): finite harmonic sums and their coefficient extraction.
1.5 Lost at c (printed pp. 10–12; PDF pp. 16–18): complex Fourier coefficients, conjugate symmetry for real signals, average value, and finite Fourier series.

1.6 Period, Frequencies, and Spectrum (printed pp. 13–15; PDF pp. 19–21): harmonic frequencies, spectral line plots, power/energy spectrum, arbitrary-period normalization, and reciprocal period/frequency spacing.

1.7 Two Examples and a Warning (printed pp. 16–20; PDF pp. 22–26): square- and triangle-wave series, infinite high-frequency content caused by jumps and corners, windowing clicks, and instrument timbre.
1.8 The Math, the Majesty, the End (printed pp. 21–25; PDF pp. 27–31): L2 energy and norm, least-squares Fourier approximation, completeness, Parseval/Rayleigh, and Riesz–Fischer.
1.9 Orthogonality (printed pp. 26–32; PDF pp. 32–38): inner products and norms for vectors and functions; orthogonality and orthonormality of complex exponentials.

1.10 Appendix: The Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality and its Consequences (printed pp. 33–35; PDF pp. 39–41): Cauchy–Schwarz, the triangle inequality, integral forms, and existence/bounds for Fourier coefficients.
1.11 Appendix: More on the Complex Inner Product (printed pp. 36–37; PDF pp. 42–43): complex inner products, Hermitian symmetry, and Cauchy–Schwarz in the complex setting.
1.12 Appendix: Best L2 Approximation by Finite Fourier Series (printed p. 38; PDF p. 44): projection proof that Fourier coefficients uniquely minimize mean-square error.
1.13 Fourier Series in Action (printed pp. 39–49; PDF pp. 45–55): heat flow, diffusion, telegraph cables, neutron diffusion, the Dirichlet kernel, impulse trains, and sound synthesis.
1.13.1 Hot enough for ya? (printed pp. 39–47; PDF pp. 45–53): derivation of the heat equation; heat on a circle; seasonal underground temperature; Thomson’s cable law; diffusion case studies.
1.13.2 A nonclassical example: What’s the buzz? (printed pp. 47–49; PDF pp. 53–55): equal-energy harmonic sums, Dirichlet kernels, concentration toward an impulse train, and spectral sound shaping.
1.14 Notes on Convergence of Fourier Series (printed pp. 50–57; PDF pp. 56–63): coefficient decay versus smoothness, uniform convergence for smooth signals, jump values, and Gibbs oscillations.
1.14.1 How big are the Fourier coefficients? (printed pp. 50–52; PDF pp. 56–58): integration-by-parts estimates linking derivative discontinuities to 1/n, 1/n², and higher-order coefficient tails.
1.14.2 Rates of convergence and smoothness (printed pp. 53–54; PDF pp. 59–60): pointwise and uniform convergence with an explicit differentiability-dependent error rate.
1.14.3 Convergence if it’s not continuous? (printed pp. 54–57; PDF pp. 60–63): sawtooth partial sums, midpoint convergence at jumps, and the persistent Gibbs overshoot.
1.15 Appendix: Pointwise Convergence vs. Uniform Convergence (printed p. 58; PDF p. 64): a moving, growing triangular spike that converges pointwise but not uniformly.

1.16 Appendix: Studying Partial Sums via the Dirichlet Kernel: The Buzz Is Back (printed pp. 59–60; PDF pp. 65–66): partial sums as convolution with the Dirichlet kernel and the sine-over-sine closed form.
1.17 Appendix: The Complex Exponentials Are a Basis for L2([0,1]) (printed pp. 61–62; PDF pp. 67–68): three-step density, uniform-convergence, and best-approximation outline for L2 completeness.
1.18 Appendix: More on the Gibbs Phenomenon (printed pp. 62–64; PDF pp. 68–70): Dirichlet-kernel reduction of square-wave overshoot to a sine-integral maximum.
Chapter 2, Fourier Transform (printed pp. 65–94; PDF pp. 71–100): derivation, inversion, transform pairs, duality, symmetry, and shift/scale rules.

2.1 A First Look at the Fourier Transform (printed pp. 65–74; PDF pp. 71–80): periodized rect functions, continuous-spectrum limiting argument, transform and inverse definitions, inversion, bandlimited signals, and Parseval.
2.2 Getting to Know Your Fourier Transform (printed pp. 75–94; PDF pp. 81–100): transform examples and operational rules.
2.2.1 Examples (printed pp. 75–79; PDF pp. 81–85): rect/sinc, triangle/sinc², one-sided exponential decay, Lorentz power profile, and independent-variable scaling.
2.2.2 For Whom the Bell Curve Tolls (printed pp. 79–81; PDF pp. 85–87): Gaussian normalization, self-transform proof, and Euler’s polar-coordinate evaluation of the Gaussian integral.
2.2.3 General Properties and Formulas (printed p. 82; PDF p. 88): transition from a transform-pair storehouse to general operational laws.
2.2.4 Fourier transform pairs and duality (printed pp. 82–85; PDF pp. 88–91): forward/inverse symmetry, reversed signals, transform iteration, and dual pairs sinc/rect and sinc²/triangle.
2.2.5 Even and odd symmetries and the Fourier transform (printed pp. 85–86; PDF pp. 91–92): reversal, conjugate symmetry, and real/imaginary parity consequences.
2.2.6 Linearity (printed p. 86; PDF p. 92): additivity and homogeneity.
2.2.7 The shift theorem (printed pp. 86–87; PDF pp. 92–93): time shifts as unit-magnitude spectral phase ramps.
2.2.8 The stretch (similarity) theorem (printed pp. 87–90; PDF pp. 93–96): reciprocal time/frequency scaling, localization tradeoff, and scaled rect transforms.
2.2.9 Combining shifts and stretches (printed pp. 90–94; PDF pp. 96–100): affine changes, shifted rects, two-sided exponentials, and general Gaussians.
Chapter 3, Convolution (printed pp. 95–136; PDF pp. 101–142): convolution theorem, filtering, differential equations, the central limit theorem, and uncertainty.
3.1 A ∗ is Born (printed pp. 95–98; PDF pp. 101–104): convolution derived from multiplication of Fourier transforms; dual multiplication/convolution rule; rect self-convolution.
3.2 What is Convolution, Really? (printed pp. 99–100; PDF pp. 105–106): LTI context, smoothing/averaging/smearing interpretations, and flip-and-drag visualization.
3.3 Properties of Convolution: It’s a Lot like Multiplication (printed pp. 101–102; PDF pp. 107–108): commutativity, associativity, distributivity, the delta identity foreshadowed, and deconvolution.

3.4 Convolution in Action I: A Little Bit on Filtering (printed pp. 102–106; PDF pp. 108–112): impulse response, transfer function, magnitude/phase effects, and ideal lowpass, bandpass, highpass, and notch filters.

3.5 Convolution in Action II: Differential Equations (printed pp. 106–116; PDF pp. 112–122): derivative theorem; constant-coefficient ODEs; infinite-rod heat kernel; telegraph-cable diffusion; periodic versus infinite heat solutions; Jacobi/Poisson identity.
3.6 Convolution in Action III: The Central Limit Theorem (printed pp. 116–127; PDF pp. 122–133): repeated self-convolution, random variables, densities, moments, independence, and density of sums.
3.7 The Central Limit Theorem: The Bell Curve Tolls for Thee (printed pp. 128–130; PDF pp. 134–136): normalized iid sums, transform-domain proof, and convergence to the standard Gaussian.
3.8 Fourier transform formulas under different normalizations (printed p. 130; PDF p. 136): how transform constants alter inversion, differentiation, and convolution formulas.
3.9 Appendix: The Mean and Standard Deviation for the Sum of Random Variables (printed pp. 131–132; PDF pp. 137–138): convolution derivation of nµ and √nσ scaling.
3.10 More Details on the Central Limit Theorem (printed p. 132; PDF p. 138): control of the Taylor remainder in the characteristic-function argument.
3.11 Appendix: Heisenberg’s Inequality (printed pp. 133–136; PDF pp. 139–142): time/frequency variances, Cauchy–Schwarz proof, Gaussian equality case, and position/momentum interpretation.
Chapter 4 — Distributions and Their Fourier Transforms
4.1 The Day of Reckoning — limits of L1 Fourier theory; sinc as the motivating failure; the route through Schwartz functions and tempered distributions
4.2 The Right Functions for Fourier Transforms — smoothness versus decay; rapidly decreasing/Schwartz functions; inversion and Parseval on S
4.3 A Very Little on Integrals — absolute integrability, dominated convergence, and power-law tests for decay
4.4 Distributions — limits versus continuous linear functionals; functions inducing distributions; delta as evaluation; compact-support test functions
4.5 A Physical Analogy for Distributions — a thermometer/test-function measurement of a heat distribution
4.6 Limits of Distributions — convergence by pairings; Gaussian, rectangle, and general unit-area approximations to delta
4.7 The Fourier Transform of a Tempered Distribution — transform by dual action; inversion; delta, constant, shifted delta, exponentials, sine, and cosine
4.8 Fluxions Finis — distributional derivatives of steps, ramps, signum, delta, and logarithm
4.9–4.10 Approximation and compatibility — every tempered distribution approximated by Schwartz-function distributions; generalized transform contains the classical transform
4.11–4.17 Operations — reversal and duality; products with smooth functions; derivative, shift, scaling, and convolution theorems; principal-value transforms
4.18 Delta Hard at Work — ideal low-, high-, and notch-filter impulse responses; Fraunhofer diffraction for one slit, two slits, and point sources
4.19–4.21 Appendices — Riemann–Lebesgue lemma; explicit smooth windows; 1/x as a Cauchy principal-value distribution
Chapter 5 — III, Sampling, and Interpolation
5.1 X-Ray Diffraction — crystals as atomic-scale diffraction gratings and reciprocal spacing in crystallography
5.2 The III Distribution — Dirac comb definition; periodizing by convolution; sampling by multiplication; scaling identity
5.3 Fourier Transform of III — Poisson summation; self-transform property; reciprocal comb spacing; crystal electron-density spectra
5.4 Periodic Distributions and Fourier Series — periodicity as shift invariance; Fourier series of III; Fourier transforms of periodic signals
5.5–5.6 Sampling Signals — bandlimitedness; impossibility of simultaneous time and band limitation; Shannon interpolation; Nyquist rate and oversampling
5.7 Interpolation More Generally — shifted sincs as an orthonormal basis; comparison with Lagrange polynomial interpolation
5.8 Finite Sampling — exact reconstruction of a finite Fourier series from 2N+1 samples; periodized-sinc identities
5.9 Troubles with Sampling — finite-record approximation, endpoint ambiguity, undersampling, and aliasing as spectral overlap
5.10–5.11 Appendices — uniqueness of the period-1 self-transforming comb; rigorous time-limited versus bandlimited impossibility
Chapter 6 — Discrete Fourier Transform
6.1–6.3 From Continuous to Discrete — sampled time/frequency grids, Riemann-sum motivation, DFT definition, vector complex exponentials, real-input symmetry, and reciprocal grid spacings
6.4 Gauss's Problem — twelve observations of Pallas fit by a finite Fourier series
6.5–6.7 DFT structure and inversion — periodic indexing; discrete deltas; roots-of-unity orthogonality; reversal, duality, inverse transform, and matrix form
6.8–6.9 DFT properties — Parseval, shifts, modulation, circular convolution, delta identities, and equivalence of any N consecutive index sets
6.10 FFT Algorithm — even/odd splitting, recursive DFT matrix factorization, butterfly stages, NlogN complexity, and bit-reversal sorting
6.11 Zero Padding — preservation of original DFT bins, denser frequency grid, and the condition that padding not erase unknown data

7.1 Linear Systems (printed pp. 295–296; PDF pp. 301–302): systems as input-output maps, additivity, homogeneity, superposition, the zero-input test, and extension from finite to infinite linear combinations.

7.2 Examples (printed pp. 296–301; PDF pp. 302–307): a catalog that links abstract linearity to multiplication, switching, sampling, matrices, dynamical systems, integral kernels, convolution, translation, and periodization.
7.2.1 Multiplying in the time domain (printed pp. 297–298): direct proportion by a fixed function, rect/unit-step switches, and sampling as multiplication by an impulse train.
7.2.2 Matrices and integrals (printed pp. 298–299): matrix multiplication, exp(At) evolution, kernels as infinite matrices, adjoints, and the Fourier transform as an integral operator.
7.2.3 Convolution: continuous and discrete (printed pp. 299–300): convolution kernels, periodic finite convolution, Toeplitz/circulant matrix structure, and shifted-delta columns.
7.2.4 Translation or shifting (printed pp. 300–301): delay/advance, convolution with shifted deltas, and periodization as convolution with an impulse train.

7.3 Cascading Linear Systems (printed pp. 301–302; PDF pp. 307–308): operator composition, block-diagram order, equivalent kernels, convolution of impulse responses, and commutativity for cascaded LTI systems.

7.4 The Impulse Response (printed pp. 302–304; PDF pp. 308–310): impulse response as L delta(x-y), the superposition theorem/Schwartz kernel theorem, uniqueness, and the continuous-basis analogy with matrix columns.

7.5 Linear Time-Invariant Systems (printed pp. 304–307; PDF pp. 310–313): time/translation invariance, convolution characterization, circulant matrices in the discrete case, and why time-varying multiplication is not LTI.

7.6 Appendix: The Linear Millennium (printed pp. 307–308; PDF pp. 313–314): three reasons for linearity's historical power—local approximation, existence/uniqueness structure, and symmetry/group structure.

7.7 Appendix: Translating in Time and Plugging into L (printed pp. 308–309; PDF pp. 314–315): delay operators, commutation L tau_b=tau_b L, cascade interpretation, and careful substitution into convolution.
7.8 The Fourier Transform and LTI Systems (printed pp. 309–311; PDF pp. 315–317): transfer functions, filters, the no-new-frequencies property, and a squaring counterexample.

7.8.1 Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions (printed pp. 309–311): frequency response, CT complex-exponential eigenfunctions, sinusoidal amplitude/phase change, Fourier-series inputs, and DFT eigenvectors that diagonalize discrete LTI systems.
7.9 Matched Filters (printed pp. 311–313; PDF pp. 317–319): white-noise model, output-noise energy, Cauchy–Schwarz SNR bound, and filter matching to a target signal.

7.10 Causality (printed pp. 313–314; PDF pp. 319–320): general, linear, and LTI formulations; causal impulse-response support; physical realizability; and legitimate noncausal processing of prerecorded/spatial data.

7.11 The Hilbert Transform (printed pp. 314–320; PDF pp. 320–326): causal transfer-function constraints, Hilbert-transform definition, principal value, quadrature phase shift, transform pairs, analytic signals, envelopes, phase, and instantaneous frequency.
7.12 Appendix: The Hilbert Transform of sinc (printed pp. 320–321; PDF pp. 326–327): derivation via sign times rect, a derivative of a scaled triangle, and the derivative/stretch theorems.
7.13 Filters Finis (printed pp. 321–330; PDF pp. 327–336): finite periodic digital filtering, data smoothing, frequency analysis, FFT efficiency, and lowpass/bandpass design.

7.13.1 Averaging in the time domain (printed pp. 322–325): least-squares interpretation of running averages, three- and five-point filters, periodic endpoint effects, modified half-weight endpoints, and nonrecursive filtering.

7.13.2 Analysis in the frequency domain (printed pp. 325–327): transfer functions of averaging filters, center lobes versus sidelobes, stronger sidelobe decay of modified averages, and FFT-based convolution complexity.

7.13.3 Find that filter (printed pp. 327–330): ideal CT/DT lowpass transfer functions, sinc/Dirichlet-like impulse responses, ringing, tapered transitions, and bandpass construction by frequency shifts.

7.14 Appendix: Geometric Series of the Vector Complex Exponentials (printed pp. 330–332; PDF pp. 336–338): componentwise geometric sums, zero-slot special handling, and sums whose powers divide the DFT length.

7.15 Appendix: The Discrete Rect and its DFT (printed pp. 332–334; PDF pp. 338–340): endpoint-normalized discrete rectangles, their DFTs for alpha=0, 1, and 1/2, and the closed-form lowpass impulse response.

8.1 Space, the Final Frontier (printed pp. 335–347; PDF pp. 341–353): vector notation, n-dimensional Fourier transform, spatial harmonics and spectra, separable functions, multidimensional rectangles, and Gaussians.

8.1.1 The Fourier transform (printed pp. 336–343): dot-product kernel, inverse transform, duality, conjugate/even/odd symmetries, zero-phase hyperplanes, spatial-frequency direction and spacing, image spectra, notch denoising, and digital watermarking.

8.1.2 Finding a few Fourier transforms: separable functions (printed pp. 343–347): tensor-product factorization, rectangular supports to products of sinc functions, anisotropic widths, and self-transforming n-dimensional Gaussians.

8.2 Getting to Know Your Higher Dimensional Fourier Transform (printed pp. 347–361; PDF pp. 353–367): multidimensional linearity, shifts, general linear stretches, rotations, convolution, deltas, radial transforms, and change-of-variable proofs.
8.2.1–8.2.2 Linearity and Shifts (printed pp. 347–349): direct generalization of linearity and vector shifts becoming dot-product phase factors.

8.2.3 Stretches (printed pp. 349–353): independent coordinate scaling, the inverse-transpose rule for arbitrary invertible matrices, rotations, parallelogram indicators, and combined shift/stretch formulas.
8.2.4–8.2.5 Convolution and delta (printed pp. 353–356): n-dimensional convolution theorems, Schwartz functions, shifted/factored deltas, delta transforms, and determinant scaling.
8.2.6 The Fourier transform of a radial function (printed pp. 356–359): polar coordinates, zeroth-order Bessel/Hankel transform, radial-to-radial symmetry, circ, and jinc.
8.2.7 A Derivation of the General Stretch Theorem (printed pp. 359–361): multidimensional change of variables, volume scaling by |det A|, dot-product transpose identity, and delta scaling.
8.3 Higher Dimensional Fourier Series (printed pp. 361–371; PDF pp. 367–377): independent periodicity, integer-lattice harmonics, coefficients on [0,1]^d, and an extended random-walk application.

8.4 III, Lattices, Crystals, and Sampling (printed pp. 371–381; PDF pp. 377–387): two-dimensional impulse trains, general lattices, unit cells, dual lattices, lattice Poisson summation, and reciprocal-space transforms.
8.4.1 The two-dimensional III (printed pp. 372–374): the integer lattice or 'bed of nails,' lattice periodization, self-duality, and the route to two-dimensional sampling.
8.4.2 Lattices in general (printed pp. 374–375): integer combinations of basis vectors, fundamental parallelograms, basis nonuniqueness, lattice area, and linear images of Z^2.

8.4.3 III for a lattice (printed pp. 375–380): lattice impulse trains, periodization and sampling, dual bases, reciprocal area, inverse-transpose construction, and Fourier transformation to the dual lattice.

8.5 Crystals (printed pp. 381–383; PDF pp. 387–389): atomic electron density as convolution with a lattice impulse train, diffraction peaks on the reciprocal lattice, projection from 3D to film, phase loss, and a macroscopic pinhole experiment.

8.6 Bandlimited Functions on R2 and Sampling on a Lattice (printed pp. 383–386; PDF pp. 389–392): square-spectrum sampling, parallelogram support, transform-based coordinate reduction, dual-lattice sample locations, and sinc reconstruction.
8.7 Naked to the Bone (printed pp. 386–388; PDF pp. 392–394): exponential attenuation in homogeneous/layered media, line integrals of density, and the tomography inverse problem.
8.8 The Radon Transform (printed pp. 388–391; PDF pp. 394–397): normal-distance line coordinates, line impulses, Radon-transform definition, and projections as parallel families.

8.9 Getting to Know Your Radon Transform (printed pp. 391–395; PDF pp. 397–401): finite-support/discontinuous densities, exact transforms of circ and a Gaussian, linearity, shifts, and Radon symmetry.

8.11 Medical Imaging: Inverting the Radon Transform (printed pp. 396–402; PDF pp. 402–408): projection-slice theorem, Fourier reconstruction, DFT sampling of projections, polar-to-Cartesian regridding, interpolation error, and a 64-by-64 Shepp–Logan brain example.

key_results: Section 1.1 (printed p. 1; PDF p. 7): the organizing principle is that every signal has a spectrum and is determined by that spectrum; Fourier analysis alternates analysis into frequency components with synthesis back to the signal.
Sections 1.3–1.6 (printed pp. 4–15; PDF pp. 10–21): a period-T signal has harmonics e^{2πint/T} and coefficients c_n=(1/T)∫_0^T f(t)e^{-2πint/T}dt; c_0 is its average value.
Sections 1.5–1.6 (printed pp. 10–15; PDF pp. 16–21): for a real signal, c_{-n}=conj(c_n); |c_n|² is the power/energy spectrum, and the spectral lines n/T are spaced 1/T apart.
Section 1.8 (printed pp. 22–25; PDF pp. 28–31): in L2([0,1]), the degree-N Fourier partial sum is the unique best trigonometric-polynomial approximation in mean-square distance.
Section 1.8 (printed p. 24; PDF p. 30): {e^{2πint}} is an orthonormal basis of L2([0,1]), so Fourier partial sums converge to f in L2.
Section 1.8 (printed pp. 24–25; PDF pp. 30–31): Parseval/Rayleigh identity ∫_0^1|f(t)|²dt=Σ_{n=-∞}^{∞}|f̂(n)|² decomposes signal energy among harmonics.
Section 1.8 (printed p. 24; PDF p. 30): Riesz–Fischer converse—every square-summable coefficient sequence is the Fourier-coefficient sequence of an L2 function.

Section 1.9 (printed pp. 29–32; PDF pp. 35–38): the function inner product (f,g)=∫_0^1 conj(f(t))g(t)dt makes complex exponentials orthonormal; f̂(n) is the projection (e_n,f) in the notes’ slot convention.
Sections 1.10–1.11 (printed pp. 33–37; PDF pp. 39–43): Cauchy–Schwarz |(f,g)|≤||f||||g|| implies the L2 triangle inequality and guarantees bounded Fourier coefficient functionals.

Section 1.12 (printed p. 38; PDF p. 44): the Pythagorean decomposition of approximation error proves equality in the best-approximation bound only when each trial coefficient equals the Fourier coefficient.

Section 1.13.1 (printed pp. 40–43; PDF pp. 46–49): Newton cooling plus conservation yields u_t=kk′u_xx; for u_t=(1/2)u_xx on a unit circle, c_n(t)=f̂(n)e^{-2π²n²t} and u is the periodic convolution of f with Green’s function Σe^{-2π²n²t}e^{2πinx}.
Section 1.13.1 (printed pp. 44–45; PDF pp. 50–51): a sinusoidal annual surface temperature produces u(x,t)=e^{-√(2π)x}sin(2πt-√(2π)x); at √(2π)x=π it is damped to e^{-π}≈0.04 and shifted six months.
Section 1.13.1 (printed pp. 45–46; PDF pp. 51–52): Thomson’s cable model v_t=(1/KC)v_xx gives pulse-peak delay t_max=(1/6)KCx², the law of squares.
Section 1.13.2 (printed pp. 47–50; PDF pp. 53–56): the Dirichlet kernel D_N(t)=Σ_{n=-N}^N e^{2πint} concentrates at integers and tends distributionally toward an integer impulse train.

Section 1.14.1 (printed pp. 50–53; PDF pp. 56–59): integration by parts links regularity to spectral decay—jumps generate O(1/n) coefficients, corners O(1/n²), and jumps in the second derivative O(1/n³), with the pattern continuing.
Section 1.14.2 (printed p. 53; PDF p. 59): if f is p-times continuously differentiable, p≥1, its partial sums converge pointwise and uniformly with max|f-S_N|≤C/N^{p-1/2}.
Section 1.14.3 (printed pp. 56–57; PDF pp. 62–63): for a piecewise C1 periodic signal, S_N(a) tends to half the sum of the left and right limits; at continuity points this is f(a).

Sections 1.14.3 and 1.18 (printed pp. 57, 62–64; PDF pp. 63, 68–70): at a square-wave jump the limiting Gibbs maximum is 1.089490… for a ±1 signal—about 9% overshoot—and the peak narrows but does not disappear.
Section 1.16 (printed pp. 59–60; PDF pp. 65–66): the partial sum is the periodic convolution S_N(t)=∫_0^1D_N(t-s)f(s)ds, with D_N(t)=sin(π(2N+1)t)/sin(πt).

Section 2.1 (printed pp. 68–73; PDF pp. 74–79): letting the period of a periodized finite-duration signal grow and scaling its Fourier coefficients by T yields Ff(s)=∫_{-∞}^{∞}f(t)e^{-2πist}dt and a continuous spectrum.
Section 2.1 (printed pp. 72–73; PDF pp. 78–79): the inverse transform F^{-1}g(t)=∫_{-∞}^{∞}g(s)e^{2πist}ds gives Fourier inversion (f̂)∨=f under suitable hypotheses.
Section 2.1 (printed pp. 73–74; PDF pp. 79–80): a signal is bandlimited when f̂(s)=0 outside a bounded frequency interval; Fourier-transform Parseval is ∫|f(t)|²dt=∫|f̂(s)|²ds.
Sections 2.1 and 2.2.1 (printed pp. 68–77; PDF pp. 74–83): canonical pairs are Π↔sinc and Λ↔sinc², with sinc(s)=sin(πs)/(πs) and Λ=Π∗Π.
Section 2.2.1 (printed pp. 77–78; PDF pp. 83–84): the one-sided decay e^{-at}u(t) transforms to 1/(a+2πis), whose power spectrum 1/(a²+4π²s²) is a Lorentz profile.
Section 2.2.2 (printed pp. 79–81; PDF pp. 85–87): the normalized Gaussian e^{-πx²} is its own Fourier transform; Euler’s double-integral/polar-coordinate argument gives ∫e^{-x²}dx=√π.
Section 2.2.4 (printed pp. 82–85; PDF pp. 88–91): duality and reversal give F²f=f^{-}, F⁴f=f, F(sinc)=Π, and F(sinc²)=Λ.

Section 2.2.5 (printed pp. 85–86; PDF pp. 91–92): Fourier transformation preserves even/odd parity; for real f, f̂(-s)=conj(f̂(s)); real even signals transform to real even functions and real odd signals to purely imaginary odd functions.
Sections 2.2.6–2.2.7 (printed pp. 86–87; PDF pp. 92–93): F is linear, and f(t+b)↔e^{2πisb}F(s), so a time shift changes phase but not spectral magnitude.
Section 2.2.8 (printed pp. 87–90; PDF pp. 93–96): stretch theorem f(at)↔|a|^{-1}F(s/a); squeezing in time stretches in frequency and vice versa.
Sections 2.2.8–2.2.9 (printed pp. 88–94; PDF pp. 94–100): Π_p(t)=Π(t/p)↔p sinc(ps); e^{-a|t|}↔2a/(a²+4π²s²); general shifted/scaled Gaussians remain Gaussian up to phase and reciprocal width.
Section 3.1 (printed pp. 96–98; PDF pp. 102–104): (g∗f)(t)=∫g(t-x)f(x)dx and F(g∗f)=Fg·Ff; dually, F(gf)=Fg∗Ff.

Sections 3.2–3.3 (printed pp. 99–102; PDF pp. 105–108): convolution is commutative, associative, and distributive; when one unit-area kernel is localized near zero it replaces f(t) by a nearby weighted average and typically smooths while spreading support.

If f∈L1(R), then Ff exists, is continuous, satisfies |Ff(s)|≤||f||1, and tends to zero as |s|→∞. These facts do not guarantee inversion or that Ff is itself integrable. [§§4.1, 4.19]

The basic pair Π↔sinc exposes the weakness of absolute-integrability theory: Π is in L1, but sinc is not, even though its oscillatory improper transform recovers Π away from the jump endpoints. [§4.1.1, printed pp. 138–140]

The Schwartz space S consists of infinitely differentiable functions whose derivatives decay faster than every power of |x|. The Fourier transform maps S to itself, Fourier inversion holds on S, and Parseval's identity is valid there. [§4.2]

Repeated integration by parts makes the smoothness/decay tradeoff precise: derivatives of f become powers of frequency multiplying Ff, so enough smoothness and boundary decay force rapid spectral decay. [§4.2.1]

A tempered distribution is a continuous linear functional on S: it accepts a Schwartz test function and returns a complex number. Ordinary functions of at most polynomial growth induce tempered distributions by integration against the test function. [§4.4.2–4.4.3]
Delta is defined without assigning it a pointwise infinity: ⟨δ,φ⟩=φ(0), and the shifted distribution satisfies ⟨δa,φ⟩=φ(a). Convolution with delta is the identity, δ*φ=φ. [§§4.4.1–4.4.3]

If fn distributions converge on every test function, their pointwise pairing limit defines a distribution. Any unit-area f yields the delta approximation fp(x)=pf(px)→δ as p→∞; Gaussian and shrinking-rectangle families are special cases. [§§4.6–4.6.1]

The generalized Fourier transform is defined by dual action, ⟨FT,φ⟩=⟨T,Fφ⟩, with the analogous inverse definition. Fourier inversion then holds for every tempered distribution in a few lines because it already holds for Schwartz functions. [§4.7.1]

Generalized transform pairs include Fδ=1, F1=δ, Fδa=e^{−2πisa}, and F(e^{2πiax})=δa. Thus eternal sinusoids acquire discrete line spectra even though their classical Fourier integrals diverge. [§4.7.2]
Under the notes' normalization, F(cos 2πax)=1/2(δa+δ−a) and F(sin 2πax)=1/(2i)(δa−δ−a); the former is real/even and the latter imaginary/odd. [§4.7.2]
The distributional derivative is defined by ⟨T′,φ⟩=−⟨T,φ′⟩, and higher derivatives transfer with alternating sign. Consequently H′=δ, the ramp derivative is H, sgn′=2δ, and ⟨δ′,φ⟩=−φ′(0). [§4.8]

The generalized transform genuinely extends the classical one: whenever f and its classical Ff induce distributions, the distribution induced by Ff equals the generalized transform of the distribution induced by f. [§4.10]
A smooth function can multiply a distribution through ⟨gT,φ⟩=⟨T,gφ⟩. In particular g(x)δa=g(a)δa, so xδ=0; conversely, any distribution T satisfying xT=0 is cδ. [§4.13]
The derivative theorem survives unchanged in form: F(T′)=2πis FT and (FT)′=F(−2πixT). Combined with parity, it gives F(sgn)=1/(πis), with 1/s interpreted as a principal value. [§4.14]
Further principal-value pairs are F(1/x)=−πi sgn(s) and FH=1/2[δ+1/(πis)]. The apparent 1/x function acts by a symmetric Cauchy principal-value pairing near zero. [§4.14.1, §4.21]

For distributions, translation and scaling are defined through their action on oppositely translated or reciprocally scaled test functions. The familiar laws follow: F(τbT)=e^{−2πibs}FT, F(T(ax))=|a|^{−1}(FT)(s/a), and δ(ax)=|a|^{−1}δ(x). [§§4.15–4.16]

Convolution is not defined for every pair of distributions, but a test function ψ may convolve with a distribution T, and F(ψ*T)=(Fψ)(FT). Delta identities include δa*δb=δa+b and δ^(n)*f=f^(n). [§4.17]

Ideal high-pass and notch impulse responses require delta terms: high(t)=δ(t)−2νc sinc(2νct), while a symmetric notch centered at ±ν0 has notch(t)=δ(t)−4νc cos(2πν0t)sinc(2νct). Both act by subtracting selected content from the original signal. [§4.18.1]

Under the Fraunhofer far-field approximation, the complex electric field versus p=sinθ/λ is proportional to the Fourier transform of the aperture A(x); observed intensity is proportional to |FA|². [§4.18.2]

A slit of width a produces intensity a²sinc²(a sinθ/λ). Two width-a slits separated by b multiply that envelope by 4cos²(πb sinθ/λ), while two point sources leave only the cosine-squared fringes. [§4.18.2, printed pp. 203–205]

A smooth compact window can be built explicitly from flat exponential pieces and scaled to cut off a signal without introducing endpoint discontinuities; the notes use this to justify inversion and approximation arguments. [§4.20]
The Dirac comb IIIp=Σkδ(x−kp) has two complementary actions: f*IIIp=Σkf(x−kp) periodizes by addition, while f·IIIp=Σkf(kp)δ(x−kp) samples at spacing p. [§§5.2.1–5.2.2]
Comb scaling obeys III(px)=p^{−1}III1/p(x) for p>0. This reciprocal scaling is the first sign that a lattice and its frequency-domain counterpart have inverse spacings. [§5.2.3]
Poisson summation states Σkφ(k)=ΣkFφ(k) for Schwartz φ. It implies the central identity FIII=III and, after scaling, FIIIp=p^{−1}III1/p. [§5.3]

A one-dimensional crystal density ρp=ρ*IIIp transforms to (Fρ/p)III1/p. Diffraction spots therefore sample the atomic form factor at spacing 1/p, so measured spot spacing is reciprocal—not directly proportional—to atomic spacing. [§5.3.1]
A distribution is p-periodic when τpS=S. Periodizing one period φ=ΠpΦ gives Φ=φ*IIIp, and Fourier transformation yields the usual Fourier-series coefficients as samples of Fφ at k/p. [§5.4]

A signal is bandlimited to bandwidth p when its transform vanishes outside |s|<p/2. No nonzero signal can be both time-limited and bandlimited; in fact a bandlimited signal zero on any open interval is identically zero. [§5.5.1, §§5.6 and 5.11]
For a signal with Ff(s)=0 on |s|≥p/2, exact Shannon interpolation is f(t)=Σk f(k/p)sinc[p(t−k/p)]. The sample spacing is 1/p and reconstruction uses infinitely many samples. [§5.6]

If the nonzero spectrum reaches ±νmax, reconstruction requires a sampling rate greater than 2νmax; oversampling replaces p by any larger q and supplies more closely spaced samples than strictly necessary. [§5.6]

The shifted functions {sinc(t−n)} form an orthonormal basis for L2 signals bandlimited to [−1/2,1/2]. Each sample g(n) is exactly the projection ⟨g,sinc(t−n)⟩, making interpolation an orthogonal expansion rather than merely curve fitting. [§5.7]

A q-periodic finite Fourier series with harmonics −N through N is determined by M=2N+1 samples spaced q/M apart. Its exact sampling rate is 2νmax+νmin, and its interpolation kernel is a ratio of sincs. [§5.8]

The periodized-sinc identity Σk sinc(pt−kpq)=[1/(pq)]sin((2N+1)πt/q)/sin(πt/q), with N the largest integer below pq/2, converts an infinite sampling sum into a finite Fourier kernel. The special case Σn sinc(t−n)=1 is highlighted. [§5.8]

Aliasing is the failure of Ff=Πq(Ff*IIIq) when the sampling rate q is below bandwidth: shifted spectral replicas overlap before cutoff. Distinct signals then have identical samples and cannot be distinguished from those samples alone. [§5.9.1]
At one sample per second, cos(9πt/2) aliases to cos(πt/2): their integer samples agree because the original 9/4-Hz line folds to 1/4 Hz after periodization. [§5.9.1, printed pp. 238–241]

Sampling exactly at an endpoint can be signal-dependent: sin(2πt) sampled at 2 Hz can alias to zero, while cos(2πt) at the same rate is recoverable when boundary deltas are cut with half weight. The notes recommend treating such endpoint cases separately. [§5.9.2]
Up to scale, III is uniquely characterized as a period-1 tempered distribution that equals its Fourier transform; normalizing its zeroth Fourier coefficient to one makes it unique. [§5.10]

Starting with an approximately time-limited and bandlimited signal, N=2BL samples and Riemann-sum discretization motivate the DFT. Time and frequency grids satisfy ΔtΔν=1/N, so for fixed N refining one grid coarsens the other. [§§6.1 and 6.3]
For f[0],…,f[N−1], the DFT is F[m]=Σ_{n=0}^{N−1}f[n]e^{−2πimn/N}. It is a linear map CN→CN whose matrix entries are powers of the Nth root of unity. [§§6.2 and 6.5]

DFT inputs and outputs extend naturally as N-periodic sequences, and the transform can be computed over any N consecutive indices. Honest negative indices map by periodicity to bins N/2+1 through N−1. [§§6.6 and 6.9]
For real input and even N, the DFT has conjugate symmetry: bins above N/2 mirror the positive-frequency bins, F[0] is the sample sum, and F[N/2] is the real alternating sample sum. [§6.2.1]
The discrete delta and roots of unity satisfy Fδk=ω^{−k}, F(ω^k)=Nδk, and ω^k·ω^l=N when k≡l mod N and zero otherwise. These orthogonality relations give the inverse DFT. [§§6.7.1–6.7.2]
DFT duality is F(f−)=(Ff)− and FFf=Nf−. Therefore F−1f=(1/N)F(f−)=(1/N)(Ff)−, or f[n]=(1/N)ΣkF[k]e^{2πikn/N}. As matrices, F*F=NI. [§§6.7.3–6.7.5]
DFT Parseval is (Ff)·(Fg)=N(f·g), hence ||Ff||²=N||f||². Shift and modulation dualize as F(τpf)=ω^{−p}Ff and F(ω^nf)=τn(Ff). [§6.8]
Discrete convolution is circular: (f*g)[m]=Σ_{k=0}^{N−1}f[k]g[m−k], with indices modulo N, and F(f*g)=(Ff)(Fg). Conversely, F(fg)=N^{−1}(Ff*Fg). [§6.8.1]
The radix-2 FFT splits the DFT into transforms of even and odd indexed inputs, then recombines them with twiddle factors: F[m]=E[m]+ωN^{−m}O[m] and F[m+N/2]=E[m]−ωN^{−m}O[m]. [§6.10.1]

Recursively factoring N=2^n transforms gives C(N)=2C(N/2)+KN and therefore C(N)=KNlog2N, instead of order N². For N=1024 the notes compare roughly one million direct operations with about ten thousand FFT-scale operations. [§6.10.2]

Radix-2 input sorting is bit reversal: write each index in fixed-width binary, reverse its bits, and feed the corresponding sample into that slot. Butterfly matrices then perform the staged recombinations. [§6.10.3]

If an N-point sequence is padded to M=kN, every original DFT bin survives as F[m]=G[km], while the frequency-grid spacing shrinks by 1/k without changing total frequency extent. Padding refines sampled display points; it is justified only when the omitted time samples are truly zero. [§6.11]

pedagogy: Osgood teaches Fourier analysis as a connected problem-solving narrative rather than a catalog of transform pairs. Concrete phenomena—periodic waves, music, heat flow, filtering, probability, diffraction, sampling, image noise, crystallography, random walks, and tomography—motivate the mathematics; detailed derivations then turn those observations into definitions and structural theorems. The recurring moves are geometric projection, analogy between finite-dimensional linear algebra and function spaces, translation between time/space and frequency, and careful comparison of continuous, distributional, discrete, and multidimensional formulations. Formal proofs are given for central algebraic and analytic identities, while difficult measure-theoretic, topological, convergence, or existence questions are explicitly deferred or isolated in appendices. Warnings about normalization, variables, conjugation, indexing, endpoint conventions, unjustified integrals, and physical interpretation function as metacognitive instruction. Exercises are mostly embedded prompts to show, check, draw, compute a small case, or explain a formula in words rather than end-of-chapter sets; worked examples and long application arcs carry much of the practice. The course assumes calculus, differential equations, complex numbers, linear algebra, multiple integration, and growing comfort with probability and computation, while Appendix A supplies a compact complex-number review and Appendix B an annotated path to deeper sources.

gems: Section 1.1 (printed p. 1; PDF p. 7): the course’s compact north star—every signal has a spectrum and is determined by it—sets up analysis and synthesis as the two directions of the subject.

Section 1.2 (printed pp. 3–4; PDF pp. 9–10): blue and yellow stripe fields appear greenish when spatial frequency is high, turning Fourier resolution into a perceptual experiment and raising a hysteresis/orientation question.
Section 1.6 (printed pp. 15–16; PDF pp. 21–22): 'larger period in time, smaller spacing of the spectrum' is an aphorism that anticipates both the transform limit and time/frequency reciprocity.

Section 1.7 (printed pp. 16–20; PDF pp. 22–26): square waves need arbitrarily high frequencies because finite sinusoid sums are continuous; triangle corners still force infinite terms because finite sums are smooth. Sharp window cuts therefore produce audible clicks.

Sections 1.7–1.8 (printed pp. 20–21; PDF pp. 26–27): bassoon and flute spectra explain different timbre on the same note, while the oboe’s unusually rich harmonics make it useful for orchestral tuning because every instrument can find something of itself in the oboe.

Section 1.8 (printed p. 26; PDF p. 32): the John Tukey paraphrase—one would not want to fly in a plane whose design depended on Riemann versus Lebesgue integrability—deflates a difficult analytic caveat without hiding it.

Section 1.9 (printed pp. 26–27; PDF pp. 32–33): Osgood’s practical Pythagorean-theorem story lays out a rectangular field by checking a diagonal, then transfers that geometric orthogonality intuition to functions.

Section 1.13.1 (printed p. 45; PDF p. 51): underground seasonal temperature at the depth √(2π)x=π has only e^{-π}≈4% amplitude and is six months out of phase—mathematical proof of why a cellar stays steady and reverses the seasons.

Section 1.13.1 (printed pp. 45–47; PDF pp. 51–53): Thomson’s 1855 law of squares says 1,000 cable miles impose 100 times the delay of 100 miles, not 10. The first Atlantic cable ignored the model, used too much voltage, and failed after three weeks: 'They fried it.'

Section 1.13.1 (printed p. 47; PDF p. 53): neutron-diffusion models gave about 60 kg of U-235 in a 9 cm radius sphere, versus 200 kg from a cruder model; the discrepancy becomes a high-stakes lesson in model accuracy.

Section 1.13.2 (printed pp. 47–50; PDF pp. 53–56): summing every harmonic with equal energy creates the 'continuous-time buzz'; its Dirichlet-kernel peaks tend toward an impulse train, bridging sound synthesis and sampling.

Section 1.14.3 (printed pp. 56–57; PDF pp. 62–63): Michelson and Stratton’s mechanical Fourier-series drawing machine produced jump ripples they blamed on machinery; Gibbs showed the fixed ~9% overshoot was mathematics, not a broken device.
Section 1.18 (printed pp. 62–64; PDF pp. 68–70): the universal Gibbs peak emerges from (2/π)∫_0^π(sin s)/s ds and sits at t=1/(2N+1), a crisp endpoint for the Dirichlet-kernel story.
Section 2.1 (printed p. 69; PDF p. 75): after deriving rect↔sinc from ever-longer periodizations, Osgood remarks that many electrical engineers see sinc in their dreams.

Section 2.1 (printed p. 70; PDF p. 76): two actual Fry’s Electronics installations embody Fourier waveforms in a storefront and a mechanical sculpture—an unexpected pause between the rect example and the general transform limit.

Section 2.2.2 (printed pp. 80–81; PDF pp. 86–87): Euler’s famous Gaussian-integral trick squares an impossible one-dimensional integral, changes to polar coordinates, and makes the extra Jacobian factor r solve it exactly.

Section 2.2.4 (printed pp. 84–85; PDF pp. 90–91): the identity F²f=f reversed, hence F⁴=I, makes Fourier transformation a four-step cycle; Osgood notes that some people attach mystical significance to it.
Section 3.2 (printed pp. 99–100; PDF pp. 105–106): 'Convolution is what convolution does' rejects a single metaphor, then offers the more useful trio: weighted averaging, smoothing, and smearing.
Section 3.2.1 (printed p. 100; PDF p. 106): Π is discontinuous but Π∗Π=Λ is continuous; one self-convolution removes jumps while leaving corners, a minimal worked demonstration of smoothing.
Section 3.3 (printed p. 102; PDF p. 108): deconvolution appears as spectral division Fh/Fg, and zeros of Fg expose why separating a signal from noise is ill-conditioned rather than merely algebraic.

Section 3.4.1 (printed pp. 104–106; PDF pp. 110–112): an ideal sharp lowpass needs an infinite sinc impulse response and cannot be achieved exactly; highpass and notch responses remain inaccessible at this stage until delta functions arrive.

Section 3.5 (printed p. 107; PDF p. 113): a second-order ODE u''-u=-f collapses to multiplication in frequency and returns as convolution with (1/2)e^{-|t|}, putting the earlier two-sided exponential pair to work.

Section 3.5 (printed pp. 114–116; PDF pp. 120–122): a single Gaussian identity makes heat flow on a circle and on an infinite rod literally the same solution after periodization, and its x=0 special case is Jacobi’s theta identity.

Section 3.6 (printed pp. 116–118; PDF pp. 122–124): repeated convolution turns both a rectangle and a literally random jagged signal into a Gaussian-looking curve—'from seeming chaos'—before probability explains why.
Section 3.6.1 (printed p. 118; PDF p. 124): 'A random variable is a number you don’t know yet' is the deliberately informal definition that opens the probability interlude.

Section 3.6.6 (printed pp. 124–125; PDF pp. 130–131): one fair die is a six-bin rect; two dice yield a triangular distribution with six of 36 ways to make seven, so probability convolution becomes countable and visible.

Sections 3.6–3.7 (printed pp. 118, 128–130; PDF pp. 124, 134–136): the Lippmann quip—experimenters trust the normal approximation as a theorem, mathematicians as experiment—frames the CLT proof via [P(s/√n)]^n→e^{-2π²s²}.

Section 3.11 (printed pp. 133–135; PDF pp. 139–141): the time/frequency uncertainty lower bound is proved with Parseval, Cauchy–Schwarz, and one integration-by-parts trick; equality selects Gaussians yet again.

Section 3.11 (printed pp. 135–136; PDF pp. 141–142): position is multiplication by x, momentum is (1/2πi)d/dx, and their noncommutation converts the analytic variance bound into quantum measurement uncertainty.

The chapter's crisis is the field's most basic pair: Π transforms cleanly to sinc, yet sinc is not absolutely integrable. Osgood asks how multibillion-dollar industries can depend on integrals that do not converge, then rebuilds the theory instead of hiding the issue. [§4.1.1]

‘Distributions are what distributions do’ becomes a programming interface: pass a distribution a Schwartz function and it returns a number. Delta is no longer an infinite spike but the simplest nontrivial functional—evaluate at zero. [§§4.4.2–4.4.3]
The heat kernel gives delta a job before giving it mystique: as t→0+, the Gaussian solution operator g(·,t)*f tends to δ*f=f and recovers the initial temperature of an infinite rod. [§4.4.1]

Osgood calls limits-based distributions ‘vacuum tubes’ and linear-functional distributions ‘transistors’; the analogy marks a real conceptual upgrade from hazy limiting objects to precise operations on test functions. [§4.4]

Generalized Fourier inversion—the result motivating the entire chapter—takes only a few lines once the transform is defined by ⟨FT,φ⟩=⟨T,Fφ⟩. The right definition makes the hard theorem nearly automatic. [§4.7.1]

Distributional calculus vindicates the student's forbidden answer: the cornered unit ramp really does differentiate to the unit step, and the unit step differentiates to delta. A jump of height two in signum produces 2δ. [§4.8]
The identity g(x)δa=g(a)δa turns a spike into an exact sampler, while δa*δb=δa+b turns spike location into arithmetic under convolution. [§§4.13.1 and 4.17]

Ideal high-pass filtering is literally ‘original minus low-pass part’: its impulse response δ−sinc makes the verbal design visible in one equation. The notch filter repeats the same logic after modulating the sinc to ±ν0. [§4.18.1]

Fraunhofer diffraction makes the transform observable: the aperture is the time-domain signal, angle divided by wavelength is frequency, and visible brightness is the squared magnitude. A single slit displays sinc² ‘live.’ [§4.18.2]
A point aperture predicts a uniformly illuminated far field, giving an optical interpretation of Fδ=1 rather than just a distributional proof. [§4.18.2, printed p. 205]

Von Laue's 1912 proposal tested three hypotheses at once—X-rays are waves, crystals are periodic, and atomic spacing is about 10−8 cm—by using the crystal itself as the grating that could not be manufactured. [§5.1]

The book calls FIII=III ‘the deepest fact about the integers’ known to every engineer and spectroscopist. Periodicity, sampling, Poisson summation, and reciprocal lattices all collapse into that one self-transform. [§5.3]
The reciprocal-lattice warning is intentionally career-sized: mistake diffraction-spot spacing for direct atomic spacing rather than 1/p and ‘kiss your Nobel prize goodbye.’ [§5.3.1]

The sampling theorem proof is only three moves—periodize the spectrum, cut back to the original, invert—and Osgood remarks on the almost obscene efficiency with which multiplication and convolution swap roles. [§5.6]

Shifted sinc functions are not just interpolation bumps; they are an orthonormal basis, and the sample g(n) is the basis coefficient. This connects Shannon reconstruction directly back to Fourier-series projection. [§5.7]

The finite sampling formula writes cos 2πt using three sample values and a forbidding ratio of sinc functions, then a plot confirms the identity. The deliberately absurd complexity makes exact finite reconstruction memorable. [§5.8, printed p. 234]

The identity Σn sinc(t−n)=1 looks impossible term by term; a ±100 partial sum plot exposes Gibbs-like edge effects while the distributional/periodization argument explains the infinite result. [§5.8, printed p. 235]

Aliasing is shown with an exact ambush: a 9/4-Hz cosine sampled once per second is indistinguishable from a 1/4-Hz cosine, and the frequency-domain derivation shows precisely which shifted deltas land inside the reconstruction window. [§5.9.1]

The endpoint pair sin 2πt and cos 2πt makes ‘sample above twice the highest frequency’ more than pedantry: at exactly 2 Hz the sine disappears into all-zero samples while the cosine survives through half-weight boundary deltas. [§5.9.2]

The DFT begins by admitting an impossibility: computation pretends a signal is both time- and band-limited and that finitely many samples suffice. It works well enough that much of the world's economy depends on the approximation. [Chapter 6 opening; §6.1]

Gauss had twelve Pallas orbit measurements and devised the heart of an FFT-style decomposition roughly a century before Cooley and Tukey; the notes give the raw data, fitted coefficients, and modern reconstruction. [§6.4]

Merge-sort is the computational warm-up for FFT: recycling partial work changes one million squared comparisons at N=10^6 into only millions-scale NlogN work, preparing the same divide-and-conquer idea for transforms. [§6.10]
For N=1024, direct DFT scale is about 2^20≈one million operations while FFT scale is about 1024·10≈ten thousand, or roughly five thousand for real inputs. [§6.10.2]

Bit reversal turns a mysterious shuffle into a three-step rule. For N=8, reversing binary indices sends the natural order to 0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7, exactly the order needed by the butterfly stages. [§6.10.3]

Zero padding gets a careful warning: it inserts denser frequency-grid samples and preserves old bins, but it is legitimate only if the newly asserted time samples are truly zero; otherwise it destroys real data rather than adding information. [§6.11]

The chapter title for impulse response calls the Schwartz kernel theorem 'the deepest fact in the theory of distributions' while noting that every electrical engineer already knows it as superposition: a delta-basis decomposition turns any linear system into an integral kernel. [Sec. 7.4, printed pp. 302–304]

A boss asks for a convolution model of a switch. The answer is no: multiplication by a time-varying rect is linear but not time invariant. Osgood then computes its two-variable impulse response anyway and verifies the superposition integral. [Sec. 7.5, printed pp. 306–307]
The nonlinear squaring test is ruthlessly compact: feed in one 1 Hz cosine and get DC plus 2 Hz, making 'LTI adds no frequencies' memorable by violation. [Sec. 7.8, printed p. 309]

The DFT exponentials do more than simplify convolution: they are an orthogonal eigenbasis for every discrete LTI operator, so they literally diagonalize every circulant matrix. [Sec. 7.8.1, printed p. 311]

Matched filtering is not introduced as a recipe but as equality in Cauchy–Schwarz: the best possible SNR is target-signal energy divided by the white-noise level squared. [Sec. 7.9, printed pp. 311–313]

Causality is carefully separated from linearity and time invariance, then reinterpreted: optical image processing and prerecorded music can reasonably use future/spatial samples because 'everything is there already.' [Sec. 7.10, printed pp. 313–314]
Osgood jokes that convolving with 1/(pi t) is the most complicated imaginable way to turn a sine into a cosine, just after proving Hilbert(cos)=-sin and Hilbert(sin)=cos. [Sec. 7.11, printed p. 317]

The analytic-signal construction is operationally vivid: throw away negative frequencies, double positive ones, invert, and envelope and instantaneous frequency emerge from magnitude and phase. [Sec. 7.11, printed pp. 318–320]

A moving least-squares line fit through three samples unexpectedly collapses to the simple running mean; geometry, regression, convolution, and filtering become the same operation. [Sec. 7.13.1, printed pp. 322–323]

Circular convolution's endpoint surprise is made concrete: smoothing the leftmost point averages in the rightmost original sample. The 'replace a jump by its average' convention then motivates endpoint/tap changes. [Sec. 7.13.1, printed pp. 323–324]

Modified running averages deliberately trade a wider main lobe for sidelobes that die much faster, a compact lesson that 'smoother' means a measurable frequency-response choice, not just a prettier curve. [Sec. 7.13.2, printed pp. 325–327]

In two dimensions a frequency is a vector normal to stripes, and its reciprocal length is the stripe spacing. This single geometry explains orientation, period, and why spectra of real stripe images contain paired dots. [Sec. 8.1.1, printed pp. 338–341]

Periodic stripes obscure an aircraft, but they create compact outlying spectral features; blacking out those features and inverting makes the plane reappear, imperfectly enough to expose the method's assumptions. [Sec. 8.1.1, printed pp. 341–342]

The general stretch theorem's memorable maxim is 'reciprocal means inverse transpose': a spatial transform A sends frequency coordinates through A^{-T}, while a pure rotation is the happy special case that looks identical in both domains. [Sec. 8.2.3, printed pp. 349–351]

Pólya's random-walk result arrives through Fourier series: the walker returns infinitely often with probability one in dimensions 1 and 2, yet escapes in dimension 3 and higher because the same 1/|x|^2 singularity switches from divergent to integrable. [Sec. 8.3.1, printed pp. 366–371]

For the example lattice generated by columns (3,1) and (-1,2), the unit-cell area is 7 while the dual-lattice area is 1/7; the plotted compression turns determinant reciprocity into something visible. [Sec. 8.4.2–8.4.3, printed pp. 374–379]

A macroscopic pinhole array diffracts into spots on its reciprocal lattice, a tabletop analog of X-ray crystallography that also exposes the hard missing-phase problem. [Sec. 8.5, printed pp. 381–383]

Two-dimensional sampling reverses the expected lattice: a spectrum bounded by a parallelogram set by u1,u2 requires spatial samples on the dual basis u1*,u2*, while reconstruction sincs still use the original basis in their dot products. [Sec. 8.6, printed pp. 383–386]

Tomography begins with murky water: constant percentage loss gives exponential attenuation, and taking -ln(I/I0) turns detector readings into line integrals ready for the Radon transform. [Sec. 8.7, printed pp. 386–388]

The Projection-Slice Theorem says each transformed projection is literally a radial spoke of the 2D spectrum; the practical sting is that FFTs want a Cartesian grid, and polar-to-Cartesian interpolation is identified as the largest reconstruction error. [Sec. 8.11, printed pp. 397–400]

The concluding model brain uses only 64 angles by 64 ray samples. Its visibly blocky reconstruction makes the theory-to-algorithm gap an artifact learners can inspect rather than an abstract warning. [Sec. 8.11, printed pp. 401–402]

Appendix A dispatches a common misconception: two sinusoids of the same frequency but different phase do not beat; their phasors form a rigidly rotating parallelogram whose diagonal is one sinusoid at the same frequency. [Appendix A.4, printed pp. 411–412]
